subject: english-language
title: Intersectionality and Identity
welcome_lead: Gender does not act alone. Crenshaw, Eckert and queer linguistics open the field to multiple intersecting identities.
meta_desc: Intersectionality, communities of practice and queer linguistics at A-Level English Language.
final_note: You have moved beyond binary categories to intersectional, performative analyses of identity in talk.

concepts.def: Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) — identities intersect; gender combines with race, class, sexuality and age in language use.
Eckert & McConnell-Ginet (1992) — gender is produced within local groups, not by sex alone.
Research into how LGBTQ+ speakers construct identity through language; rejects fixed gay/straight binaries.
Linguistic features index stances and qualities (toughness, care) that become associated with gendered identities.
A speaker's positioning (epistemic, affective) within talk — central to performative gender.
Bundles of features used to project an identity in a context (Eckert third wave).

walkthroughs.body_html: Crenshaw argued that a Black woman's experience is not a sum of woman plus Black but a distinct intersection. In language, a Black British teenage girl's MLE features perform several identities simultaneously.
Within a friendship group, a hedge can index thoughtfulness; in another it might index doubt. Eckert urges analysis at the level of practice — what features mean here, with these people.

Queer linguistics, drawing on Butler, treats sexual identity as performative. Lavender linguistics studies in-group features (lexis, intonation) used to signal identity within and across LGBTQ+ communities.

mcqs.q: Are claims that women use more 'tentative' language well-supported?
options: Women always use more hedges and tag questions than men.
Early studies (Lakoff) made broad claims, but later research (e.g. Holmes, Cameron) shows context matters more than gender, and many supposed differences disappear with proper data.
Chomsky said children should be taught grammar from age two.
Women and men have different vocal cords so speak differently.
